title: Rust Ownership: Moves, Copy, Drop Order & Function Calls
summary: A dense field guide to Rust's ownership model — how values move, which types copy, when destructors run and in what order, and how ownership flows through function calls, closures and collections. Covers the mechanics the compiler enforces, the errors it emits, and the idioms that make ownership ergonomic.

chapters.title: 1. Ownership Fundamentals
points: Definition: every value in Rust has exactly one owner variable at any moment.
Rule 1: one owner. Rule 2: exactly one owner at a time. Rule 3: owner goes out of scope, value is dropped.
Ownership is a compile-time discipline — zero runtime cost, no GC, no refcount unless you opt in with Rc/Arc.
Scope = the block `{ }` a binding lives in; `let s = String::from("hi");` owns the heap buffer until end of block.
Stack vs heap: `String` is a 3-word stack header (ptr, len, capacity) pointing at a heap buffer; `i32` lives entirely on the stack.
Example: `{ let s = String::from("hi"); } // s dropped here, heap buffer freed`.
RAII: acquisition is initialization, release is scope exit — Rust inherits this from C++ but enforces it statically.
Ownership solves double-free: only one owner may free, so `free` runs exactly once.
Ownership solves use-after-free: a moved-out or dropped binding is statically unusable.
Ownership solves data races: aliasing XOR mutation is checked at compile time.
Three ways to hand a value on: move (transfer), copy (bitwise duplicate), borrow (&T / &mut T, temporary access).
Ownership applies to any resource, not just memory: files, sockets, locks, GPU handles all use the same drop mechanism.
Comparison: C manual free / C++ RAII+copy-ctors / Java-Python GC / Rust compile-time ownership.
Non-lexical lifetimes (NLL): since Rust 2018 a borrow ends at last use, not end of block — errors are narrower than the old rules.

chapters.title: 2. Moves: The Default Transfer
points: Assignment of a non-Copy value is a move, not a copy: `let a = String::from("x"); let b = a;` moves.
After a move the source binding is invalidated — the compiler marks it 'moved out of'.
Canonical error: `error[E0382]: borrow of moved value: `a``, with note `move occurs because `a` has type `String`, which does not implement the `Copy` trait`.
Shallow bitwise copy at machine level: the 3-word header is memcpy'd; the heap buffer is NOT duplicated.
Move is a memcpy the optimizer usually elides — moves are cheap, no deep clone happens implicitly.
Only one of the two bindings will run drop, so no double-free: the source is statically dead.
Rust has no 'move constructor' hook — moves are always a plain bit copy, unlike C++ where a move can run user code.
Corollary: Rust values may not be self-referential across a move; that is why `Pin` exists for futures.
`clone()` is the explicit deep-copy escape hatch: `let b = a.clone();` — both bindings stay valid, heap buffer duplicated.
Clone is never implicit; you always see the cost at the call site.
Moves out of struct fields are partial moves: `let name = person.name;` moves that one field, leaving `person` partially moved.
After a partial move the whole struct cannot be used, but the untouched fields still can.
Cannot move out of an index or a reference: `v[0]` (E0507 'cannot move out of index'); use `v.remove(0)`, `std::mem::take`, or `.clone()`.
Cannot move out of a type that implements Drop — the destructor must see the full value.
Reassignment drops the old value first: `s = String::from("new");` frees the previous buffer immediately.

chapters.title: 3. Copy and Clone Types
points: `Copy` marker trait: values are duplicated bitwise on assignment; the source stays valid.
`Copy: Clone` — Copy is a subtrait of Clone, so you must derive or impl both: `#[derive(Clone, Copy)]`.
Copy types: all integers (`i8`..`u128`, `usize`), floats (`f32`, `f64`), `bool`, `char`, raw pointers, `&T` shared references.
Tuples and arrays are Copy iff every element type is Copy: `(i32, bool)` is Copy, `(i32, String)` is not.
NOT Copy: `String`, `Vec<T>`, `Box<T>`, `HashMap`, `&mut T`, any type owning heap memory or a resource.
`&mut T` is deliberately not Copy — copying it would create two aliasing mutable references.
A type implementing `Drop` can never be `Copy` — the compiler rejects both on one type (E0184); duplicating a value with a destructor would double-drop.
Example: `let a = 5; let b = a; println!("{a} {b}");` compiles fine — `i32` is Copy.
Copy is about semantics, not size: `[u8; 4096]` is Copy and expensive; `String` is 24 bytes and is not Copy.
Guideline: derive Copy only for small, plain-data, semantically-duplicable types — adding then removing it is a breaking API change.
`Clone` = explicit, possibly-expensive duplication via `fn clone(&self) -> Self`.
Clone can be deep (Vec allocates a new buffer) or cheap (`Rc::clone` only bumps a refcount).
Idiom: `Rc::clone(&x)` over `x.clone()` to make refcount-bump intent visible at the call site.
`Clone` can be derived when all fields are Clone; hand-written impls exist for custom sharing semantics.
Comparison row — move: source dead, no cost / Copy: source alive, implicit bit copy / Clone: source alive, explicit, may allocate.

chapters.title: 4. Ownership Across Function Calls
points: Passing by value moves the argument into the function's parameter — the caller loses it.
`fn consume(s: String) {}` then `consume(s); println!("{s}");` fails with E0382 'borrow of moved value'.
Copy arguments are duplicated instead: `fn takes(n: i32)` leaves the caller's `n` usable.
Returning a value moves ownership back out to the caller: `fn make() -> String { String::from("hi") }`.
The give-back pattern: `fn f(s: String) -> String { s }` — clunky; the tuple variant `-> (String, usize)` is why borrowing exists.
Borrow instead: `fn len(s: &String) -> usize` reads without taking ownership — the caller keeps the value.
`&mut` parameter borrows mutably: `fn push(v: &mut Vec<i32>)`, called as `push(&mut v)`.
API design rule: take `T` when you must store or consume it, `&T` to read, `&mut T` to modify in place.
Prefer `&str` over `&String` and `&[T]` over `&Vec<T>` in parameters — deref coercion makes them strictly more general.
Method receivers encode the same choice: `self` consumes, `&self` reads, `&mut self` mutates.
Consuming `self` powers builder chains (`fn name(mut self) -> Self`) and conversions (`into_iter`, `into_bytes`).
Naming convention: `into_*` consumes, `to_*` clones, `as_*` borrows a cheap view.
Constructor arguments usually take ownership: `Vec::push(&mut self, value: T)` moves the value into the vector.
Returned references borrow from an input, requiring lifetimes: `fn first(s: &str) -> &str`.
Struct-update syntax `Foo { a, ..old }` moves the remaining fields out of `old` unless they are Copy.

chapters.title: 5. Drop: Destructors and the Drop Trait
points: `Drop` trait has one method: `fn drop(&mut self)`, run automatically when the value goes out of scope.
Example: `impl Drop for Guard { fn drop(&mut self) { println!("dropping {}", self.name); } }`.
You can never call `.drop()` manually — E0040 'explicit use of destructor method'; use `drop(x)` instead.
`std::mem::drop` is literally `fn drop<T>(_x: T) {}` — it takes ownership and lets the value fall out of scope.
Drop glue: after your `drop` body runs, the compiler recursively drops every field — nested resources free automatically.
Order is fixed: the outer value's `drop` first, then its fields, in declaration order.
Drop-then-free: `Vec<T>` drops every element, then frees its buffer.
`_` is not a binding — `let _ = lock.lock();` drops the guard immediately; `let _guard = ...` keeps it alive. Classic deadlock bug.
A leading-underscore name like `_guard` still binds and still lives to end of scope, unlike bare `_`.
Temporaries drop at the end of the enclosing statement (the `;`), not the end of the block — hence surprising early releases in `match` scrutinees and method chains.
`ManuallyDrop<T>` and `mem::forget` suppress the destructor — leaking is safe in Rust, unsoundness is not.
Drop is used for RAII resources: `File` closes the handle, `MutexGuard` unlocks, `TcpStream` closes the socket, `Box` frees the allocation.
Panics run drops while unwinding — this is how Rust stays leak-free through failure paths.
A panic inside `drop` during unwinding aborts the process; keep destructors infallible.
Drop cannot return a value or an error — for fallible cleanup expose an explicit `close()` and drop as a fallback.

chapters.title: 6. Drop Order Rules
points: Local variables drop in reverse declaration order — the block behaves like a stack (LIFO).
Example: `let a = G("a"); let b = G("b");` prints `dropping b` then `dropping a`.
Why reverse: later bindings may borrow earlier ones, so they must die first.
Struct fields drop in *declaration* order — forward, not reverse. Opposite of locals; a classic trap.
Tuple elements and array/Vec elements also drop front-to-back, in index order.
Enum variants drop the active variant's fields in declaration order.
Function parameters drop in reverse declaration order after the body ends, like locals.
Temporaries within one statement drop in reverse creation order at the statement's semicolon.
Nested scopes drop entirely at the inner `}` — use a bare `{ }` block to release a lock guard early.
`drop(x)` forces an early drop by moving the value into a function that immediately ends.
A moved-out value drops at the new owner's scope end, not the original binding's.
Conditional moves are tracked by a hidden drop flag on the stack when the compiler cannot prove statically whether a value was moved.
`let` in the middle of a block starts a new sub-scope for later statements — declaration position controls lifetime.
Shadowing does NOT drop the shadowed value early: `let s = ...; let s = ...;` — the first still lives to end of scope.
Static and thread-local destructors are not guaranteed to run at process exit — do not rely on them for flushing.

chapters.title: 7. Ownership in Collections, Closures and Threads
points: `Vec<T>` owns its elements; dropping the Vec drops every element then frees the buffer.
`push(value)` moves the value in; `pop()` moves it back out as `Option<T>`.
You cannot move out of `v[0]` (E0507) — use `remove`, `swap_remove`, `std::mem::take`, `std::mem::replace`, or `drain`.
Three iterators, three ownership modes: `iter()` yields `&T`, `iter_mut()` yields `&mut T`, `into_iter()` consumes and yields `T`.
`for x in v` calls `into_iter()` and consumes `v`; `for x in &v` borrows and leaves `v` usable — the single most common beginner move error.
HashMap: `insert` moves both key and value; `remove` moves the value back out; `entry` API mutates in place.
`Option::take()` swaps in `None` and hands you the owned value — the standard trick to move out of `&mut self`.
Closures capture by least-restrictive mode: by reference, then by mutable reference, then by move, depending on use.
`move` keyword forces capture by value — required for `thread::spawn` and any closure outliving its frame.
`Fn` borrows captures, `FnMut` mutates them, `FnOnce` consumes them and can be called only once.
`thread::spawn` requires `'static` closures — the spawned thread may outlive the caller, so captures must be owned or leaked.
`Rc<T>` gives shared ownership with a non-atomic refcount, single-threaded only; drop decrements, hits zero, frees.
`Arc<T>` is the atomic, thread-safe counterpart; combine with `Mutex<T>` for shared mutation across threads.
`Rc`/`Arc` cycles leak — the count never reaches zero; break with `Weak<T>`.
`Box<T>` is single ownership on the heap; `Box::leak` gives `&'static mut T` by deliberately skipping drop.

chapters.title: 8. Common Mistakes and Compiler Errors
points: E0382 'use of moved value' — passed a `String` to a function then used it; fix by borrowing, cloning, or returning it.
E0505 'cannot move out of `x` because it is borrowed' — a live reference blocks the move; end the borrow first.
E0507 'cannot move out of borrowed content' — moving a field through `&self`; use `clone`, `take`, or change the receiver to `self`.
E0499 'cannot borrow `x` as mutable more than once' — two `&mut` alive at once; split the scopes or use `split_at_mut`.
E0502 'cannot borrow as mutable because it is also borrowed as immutable' — classic `v.push(v[0])` shape.
E0106 'missing lifetime specifier' — returning a reference not tied to any input.
Moving in a loop: `for _ in 0..3 { consume(s); }` fails — the value is gone after iteration one; clone inside or move the loop.
Trap: `for x in v` then using `v` afterwards — write `for x in &v`.
Trap: `let _ = mutex.lock().unwrap();` releases the lock instantly and silently breaks the critical section.
Trap: cloning to silence the borrow checker — works, but hides an ownership design that wanted `&` or a restructure.
Trap: assuming struct fields drop in reverse order — they drop in declaration order.
Trap: `Rc<RefCell<T>>` moves borrow checking to runtime; a double `borrow_mut()` panics instead of failing to compile.
Trap: returning a reference to a local — the local dies at the return; return the owned value instead.
Trap: self-referential structs — a move invalidates the internal pointer; use indices, `Pin`, or an arena.
Fix ladder, in order of preference: borrow → restructure ownership → `mem::take`/`replace` → clone → `Rc`/`Arc`.

chapters.title: 9. Trade-offs, Performance and Design
points: Ownership costs zero at runtime: no GC pauses, no refcount traffic, no tracing — all checks are erased after compile.
The cost is paid in compile time and in programmer effort while learning the model.
Move is a memcpy of the stack part only; LLVM elides most of them, so returning a large `Vec` is cheap.
Return value optimization: `fn make() -> BigStruct` typically constructs in place at the caller, no copy.
Clone is O(n) and allocates; Copy of a big array is O(size) but never allocates; borrowing is free.
`Rc`/`Arc` costs: 2 words of overhead plus a refcount update per clone/drop; `Arc` uses atomics and can contend across cores.
Prefer borrowing in hot loops; prefer owning in APIs that store data or cross a thread boundary.
Ownership guarantees no double-free, no use-after-free, no data race — statically, without a runtime.
It does NOT prevent memory leaks, deadlocks, logic bugs, or unbounded growth — leaking is safe Rust.
Comparison — Rust move: bit copy, source dead / C++ move: runs a move constructor, source left valid-but-unspecified.
Comparison — Rust: compile-time single owner / Swift ARC: runtime refcount on every class instance / Go and Java: tracing GC.
Fighting the borrow checker usually means the data model is wrong: consider indices, arenas, an ECS, or interior mutability.
Cloning is a legitimate engineering choice when the value is small or the code is cold — measure before contorting.
`unsafe` opts out of the checks, not out of the rules — aliasing invariants still hold and violating them is UB.
Design heuristic: make the owner the thing with the longest, clearest lifetime; everything else borrows from it.

chapters.title: 10. Summary and Quick Reference
points: One owner, one drop, at scope exit — the whole model in six words.
Non-Copy assignment moves and kills the source; Copy assignment duplicates and keeps it.
Copy types: integers, floats, `bool`, `char`, `&T`, and tuples/arrays of Copy types. Nothing owning heap memory.
`Drop` and `Copy` are mutually exclusive on the same type.
Locals drop in reverse declaration order; struct fields and tuple/array elements drop in declaration order.
Temporaries drop at the end of the statement; `drop(x)` forces an early release.
Pass by value to consume or store; pass `&T` to read; pass `&mut T` to modify.
`self` consumes, `&self` reads, `&mut self` mutates — same rule for methods.
`for x in v` consumes; `for x in &v` borrows. Memorize this one.
`move` closures own their captures — mandatory for `thread::spawn`.
Escape hatches, cheapest first: borrow, `mem::take`/`replace`, `Option::take`, `clone`, `Rc`/`Arc`.
Error cheat sheet: E0382 moved value, E0499 double mutable borrow, E0502 mixed borrows, E0505 move while borrowed, E0507 move out of borrow.
Ownership prevents double-free, use-after-free and data races; it does not prevent leaks or deadlocks.
Rule of thumb: borrow by default, own when you must store, clone when the cost is measured and small.
Next topics to study: borrowing and lifetimes, interior mutability (`Cell`, `RefCell`), and `Send`/`Sync`.
